10 Best Meal Delivery Services, Tested by an Ex-Restaurant Critic

📅 01 Feb 2020 | ⏱️ 39 min read (7862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~39 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best meal delivery services and meal kits make your home life easier—and maybe make dinner something to look forward to rather than dread.
  • Industry observers note that the best meal kits help you climb out of a cooking rut of turning to the same dishes—and the same flavors—over and over.
  • Sources indicate that but depending on your priorities, other meal delivery services might be a better option.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meal delivery services and meal kits make your home life easier—and maybe make dinner something to look forward to rather than dread. Our lead tester for this guide, former WIRED Reviews writer Matthew Korfhage, didn’t expect to appreciate meal kits as much as he did, especially since he likes to cook and worked as a food critic on both coasts for more than a decade.

Industry observers note that the best meal kits help you climb out of a cooking rut of turning to the same dishes—and the same flavors—over and over. After testing every major meal delivery service over the past two years, we’ve narrowed the field to just a few of the best options for each family and diet. Quite simply, the best meals our testers have eaten from a meal kit come from Marley Spoon, which offers a path to genuinely good home-cooked meals on nights when you might otherwise feel uninspired.

Sources indicate that but depending on your priorities, other meal delivery services might be a better option. Home Chef offers the greatest flexibility for busy families while keeping prices affordable. EveryPlate is the best meal kit for people on a tight budget. For a healthful, tailored diet (including an option for true gluten-free meals), we recommend Green Chef. If you’d rather not cook at all, CookUnity is the best prepared-meal delivery service we’ve ever had the pleasure to warm up.

According to recent reports, we assessed each meal proposal’s recipes, variety, sourcing, ease of preparation, convenience, organization, packaging, ingredient quality, and suitability for different dietary restrictions and needs. We also tested the best new and innovative meal kits for those looking for alternatives to Blue Apron's or HelloFresh’s long-standing meal delivery services. And not for nothing, we sorted out some often maddeningly nontransparent pricing.

Be sure to check out our investigation into whether meal kits are sometimes cheaper than groceries when trying out new recipes, and WIRED's related guides, including Best Plant-Based Meal Kits, Best Food Gifts You Can Buy Online, Best Coffee Subscriptions, and Best Delivery Chocolate Boxes.

It has been revealed that updated November 2026: We’re retesting the kits in this guide, including special holiday offerings from meal kit makers like Marley Spoon. We’ve added some notes reflecting this in relevant sections and checked for accuracy throughout.

In the decade since it was introduced on American shores, the strength of the Martha Stewart–endorsed Marley Spoon meal delivery service has remained steadfast: It’s the cooking.

According to recent reports, the best individual meals we’ve cooked from the 20 or so kits we’ve tested over the past two years have come from Marley Spoon. A hearty, Hungarian-influenced creamy mushroom chicken; a boldly Cajun-spiced whitefish; or a delicate eggplant parm. Those meals are still on the menu.

Sources indicate that but Marley Spoon has also been evolving of late. Over the past year or two, the German-founded meal kit has added more menu items, more cosmopolitan meals with global flavors, and a greater variety of preparation times that now include a lot of 15-minute meals. It’s done this without raising the price of the meal kit this year—no mean feat amid rising food and shipping costs.

Industry observers note that the classic “Martha’s Best” recipes are now augmented by meals that emphasize convenience and global flavors. A third of the menu is now prepared, ready-to-heat meals. There are more 15-minute dishes and tray oven bakes. Marley Spoon also seems to have broadened its international fare, with takes on a Moroccan-spiced apricot and beef tagine and Indian-influenced keema matar that’s as easy to make as garam masala sloppy Joe. You can even get special holiday kits—we can confirm that the Thanksgiving feasts are excellent, and more specialty meal options abound for December holidays.

According to recent reports, still, more than other meal kits, Marley remains devoted to classical cooking technique—the sort they teach in culinary school and on Martha Stewart’s TV shows. This is no accident. When the German-founded meal kit arrived in the US, it did so with the cooking maven’s endorsement and a lot of her recipes and techniques. Recipes often call for light seasoning throughout the process—not all at once. A deeply savory kale and sausage soup might be balanced with acid from a surprising splash of red wine vinegar.

In a recent development, marley Spoon is more honest than most meal kits about the time it actually takes to cook a recipe. While your 15-minute meal might acccctually still require 20 minutes, it definitely won’t take 30 or 40. There is one point of inconvenience with Marley, one that might help keep the organization’s prices from climbing: Unlike other top-line kits, Marley sends your ingredients jumbled in a box, which reduces packaging waste but also leaves you hunting for the right spice mix or dried ingredient. The meat sourcing also isn’t as transparent as in some kits.

Sources indicate that like Blue Apron and others, Marley Spoon has recently partnered with food delivery service Misfits Market after its previous US partner, FreshRealm, filed for Chapter 11 protection. We'll be testing and monitoring to make sure Marley keeps earning its spot at the top of this list. While maintaining value, Marley Spoon offers genuinely good cooking and acts as a little school in culinary techniques. Some other meal kits on this list might offer more flexibility. Marley offers a firm backbone.

Home Chef lets you do pretty much whatever you want. Do you want two servings of two recipes, but eight servings of a third? No problem. Did you want to add an oven-ready steak meal for six to this week’s order, and only this week’s order? Also not a problem. Have a large family? Home Chef offers a cheaper family plan for batched family meals. Want fewer meals this week than your typical order? Each meal will cost a little more, but you can still cut back your order on the fly without canceling.

More than any other meal kit we’ve tested, Home Chef is optimized for convenience, down to the transparent plastic bags that house each meal’s ingredients. The recipes are finely detailed, with easy-to-follow instructions. Nutrition and allergens are listed in even finer detail online. Each recipe is classed according to difficulty, and even the theoretically highfalutin’ “culinary collection” meals aren’t hard to make or dauntingly culinary—mayhaps a stuffed chicken breast, perhaps some gnocchi.

Recent findings suggest that it’s no surprise that WIRED previously listed Home Chef as the best meal kit for beginner chefs: the recipe instructions are full of little hand-holds and extra advice. That stated, the meals we tried weren’t quite as sophisticated or as tasty as those from our top pick, Marley Spoon, nor as varied and interesting as HelloFresh. One “culinary” meal was basically a stuffed burger with seasoned fries.

But convenience, flexibility, and good administration count for a lot in this world. So do relatively low prices: $10 a meal on most standard plans and $8 a plate on the kid-friendly family plan. If you’ve got a family life with meal demands that change from week to week—which is what a lot of people looking to meal kits are trying to solve—Home Chef may be the meal kit you need.

Recent findings suggest that cookUnity is the only prepared-meal delivery service we’ve tried that has ever delivered a meal better than local restaurant takeout. Specifically, from the Seattle kitchen run by chef Gaurav Raj, former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage tried multiple Indian gravies, from butter chicken to chicken lababdar, that tasted better than what he could get at the Punjabi restaurant down the street.

Prepared meal delivery services promise a hunger-squelching holy grail: fresh meals, delivered to your door in a box that’s ready to heat and eat, minus all the effort of actually cooking it. But the results from many other prepared-meal delivery services have been mixed. Indeed, some struggle to better the TV dinners they resemble. The reason CookUnity has been a big standout is its unique business model.

In a recent development, most prepared meal intends come from a single big corporate kitchen. But CookUnity is more like a cross between a meal service and DoorDash. CookUnity enlists restaurant chefs, often big names like Jose Garces or Rick Bayless or Iron Chef contestants, to design recipes and hire cooks who make your meals out of regional commissary kitchens, and ship them never-frozen down the street. This model leads not just to quality but also to diversity of food.

Over two years of testing, we’ve tried multiple well-composed salads, a surprisingly wonderful truffled beef stroganoff, credible Filipino adobo, and Japanese-style katsu with curry that crisped up tantalizingly in an air fryer.

Menus, chefs, and (probably) results may vary depending on your region and your distance from the cooking hub. Hubs now include Fresh York, Austin, Miami, Atlanta, Los Angeles, Seattle, Chicago, and Toronto. (See the delivery map to check whether CookUnity services your area.) Korfhage had good results from the small Seattle hub, and WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe remarked the adobo flank steak and rigatoni alla vodka she scored from the Chicago hub straight-up blew her mind.

Sources indicate that prep tends to happen one of two ways: either you nuke it, or you follow the chef’s ideal stovetop or oven instructions to create optimal texture and flavor. After reheating, you might also stretch burrata cheese over your pasta or ladle cumin-forward sauce on your salmon. The meals are filling, the textures are spot-on, and the packaging is compostable and recyclable. Each meal lasts in the fridge between four and seven days from the date of delivery, through the miracle of modified atmosphere packaging.

After retesting CookUnity this year during warmer weather in Oregon, we found that meals arrived at food-safe temperatures—no small feat, given that some meals drove in from four hours away.

Sources indicate that helloFresh is pretty much synonymous with “meal kits.” It’s the biggest and one of the oldest services. It’s become a global brand, available in 18 countries. Chances are, if you’ve tried a meal kit, it’s one of the first you tried. What’s surprised us, though, is how much HelloFresh has improved since we first tried it: better sourcing and more cosmopolitan, modern recipes.

Industry observers note that the brand has become a logistics powerhouse. These days, you get seasonal or even regional ingredients, depending on where you live. Proteins are sourced from multigenerational, family-run meat purveyors. Each subscription box is also well-organized, with each recipe’s ingredients portioned into labeled bags. All you need are pots, pans, a stove, and basic oil, salt, and butter.

In a recent development, especially over the past year, HelloFresh has undergone a near-astonishing expansion of its menu. Where Korfhage lives, more than 400 menu items are available each week, spanning a truly global range of cuisines. One day, he could find himself deep in a Gambian-inspired peanut stew. The next it’s an aspirational Hainanese chicken feast, a simplified Thai-style green curry shrimp, Tex-Mex enchiladas slathered in cheese and ranchero sauce, or Guamanian-inflected chicken kelaguen. Or he can just make himself a salad, wrap, or sandwich.

This summer, HelloFresh has even offered single-order grill boxes in partnership with meat delivery service Good Chop, with 32 servings comprising burgers (six), dogs (eight), steaks (four), sausages (eight), and bacon (eight strips) for $80. (According to Korfhage, the steaks and bacon were the two best-selling points.).

Where possible, HelloFresh has even begun dabbling in seasonal ingredients, like conehead cabbage Korfhage charred on his grill last summer. In some areas, HelloFresh has even added regional dishes and ingredients. It’s an exercise in logistics that makes the home chefs a little giddy. After criticism, the company added more rice to the rice meals last year. That stated, shipping prices are up, and the per-serving price has also hiked around 50 cents this year—a tribute to the rising gas and food prices that have plagued 2026.

The global offerings don’t make much claim to authenticity, mind you. Also, HelloFresh’s 20-minute meals sometimes take as long as 40 minutes to make. But HelloFresh’s offerings look a lot like how people eat these days. They are bright, light, and lightly internationalized: with pan-Latin steak and rice bowls, beef stir-fried with ponzu and plum, Dutch-inspired orange Dijon chicken, Thai-style curries, and maybe some mango salsa atop a vaguely Southwest-y pork roast.

In a recent development, green Chef is first and foremost the organic arm of HelloFresh, assiduous enough that they sent an apology note when they had to sub in nonorganic Roma tomatoes. In a recent August test, Green Chef’s fresh ingredients and sourcing impressed as much as any meal kit we’ve tasted, including fresh herbs, seasonal fare, wild-caught sockeye salmon, and delicious (farmed) steelhead trout.

It has been revealed that the healthiest diet is the one that’s attentive to your specific needs, and this is where Green Chef shines. The meal program has a strong vegetarian and dairy-free focus and at least 10 keto meals a week. Green Chef is also among the few meal delivery services that prepare its gluten-free meals in separate facilities—backed by independent validation from the Seattle-area Gluten Intolerance Group. As of August, more than half of Green Chef's meals are gluten-free, mostly dishes like rice or quinoa that don’t need gluten rather than pale imitations of gluteny things. Green Chef even offers free phone consultation with a dietitian. (Korfhage’s counseled him on protein and fiber and directed me to the meals marked as consistent with the Mediterranean diet.).

Recent findings suggest that meals arrive well-organized, in mostly recyclable packaging. Recipes are easy to follow, though the instructions are a bit minimalist. (Read ahead, and your prep times will go down.) The proteins are flavorful. And options are international and sophisticated, from shrimp spiced with Yemeni schug to cumin-ancho meat dishes. Even in August, the most difficult time to ship perishable food, herbs and veggies had nary a wilted leaf—a difficult and rare achievement, especially for fresh herbs like the parsley in the gremolata for a Turkish-spiced steelhead trout. Overall, there are fewer options than you’ll find from HelloFresh’s flagship kit, and Green Chef is among the more expensive meal kits. But the quality and variety of ingredients reflect that.

Hungryroot has among the lowest prep times of any meal kit we’ve tested that isn’t actually pre-prepped—perfect for the friend who “doesn’t have time to cook” and instead finds their DoorDash budget ballooning. Hungryroot meals tend to take about the same amount of time to cook as to eat, 10 to 20 minutes for most meals we’ve tried.

Each meal tends to be assembled from a small number of components, with a lot of the prep already done. An organic sauce or salsa or dressing, some version of pre-mixed salad, a sprig of broccoli, a pack of sous-vide chicken or smoked pulled pork. It’s a bit like running a personal fast-casual restaurant out of your home kitchen.

It has been revealed that it’s also nice that you can customize Hungryroot to suit your needs and dietary preferences. The massive idea behind Hungryroot is to be a full-service, AI-assisted food concierge. First, Hungryroot logs all your dietary, lifestyle, and budget preferences. (Hate a mushroom? Follow a low-salt diet? Don’t like masala spices, specifically? Don’t worry.) Then it suggests a whole world of ingredients and recipes, which you can sub out from a seemingly endless list each week, depending on local ingredient availability. Usually, there’s room left over in the plan to add some fresh fruit or a sweet treat. One detriment of this ultra-customized system is that you’ve got to get pretty far through the ordering process (and enter your credit card) before seeing your personal menu. Here’s the online “cookbook” of potential menus, for those who’d like an early glimpse.

This is a bit of a game-changer for meal kits, frankly, though the scenario I just described would end up a bit expensive ($10 a serving, plus $10 shipping). And so Blue Apron also has a DoorDash-style loyalty model: Blue Apron Plus. You pay $10 a month—the price of shipping on a single order—and then shipping is free for the month. This means that if you order more than once a month, you save money by signing up. Price per meal has fanned out since the reboot, ranging from $8 a serving for lunchtime salads and wraps to $13 for hearty bakes and seafood plates. This lets you choose meals based on your budget.

In a recent development, this is an ambitious turnaround for a meal kit that WIRED reviewers had loved in the past before going through some bumps in the road under fresh ownership beginning in 2023. So far we’ve had pretty good results. Our most recent test included fun, internationalized recipes like crisp, lightly spicy bang bang chicken; bao bun burgers with shishito peppers; za’atar-spiced salmon; and an excellent, hearty shrimp and feta bake. Prep for most recipes hovered around 30 minutes. And on each, you could sub out a main protein. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck tried Blue Apron’s low-effort, assemble-and-bake meals and came away mostly impressed by the sourcing and ingredient quality—but also wondered whether the focus on simplicity led to compromises in some recipes. She couldn’t bring herself to bake raw meat for a harissa beef dish, per instructions, without first draining the grease. And so she cooked it in a skillet first.

There’d been a few ingredient hiccups in 2025 as the latest initiative rolled out, but this summer Blue Apron partnered with grocery delivery service Misfits Market as a new fulfillment and delivery partner—theoretically leading to more regional options and faster delivery. Blue Apron has also changed its packaging to be more eco-friendly. As this goes fully online, we’ll retest Blue Apron to see the results. Note that beyond main proteins, allergens and dietary restrictions can be a little difficult to navigate on Blue Apron’s site.

Sources indicate that with most plans at $7 a serving plus shipping, HelloFresh’s budget option, EveryPlate, remains the lowest-cost meal kit we've tested. And yet, this budget meal kit still uses the same proteins from local purveyors as HelloFresh’s much more expensive plan.

It has been revealed that the secret is not skimping on calories or portions, but rather simplicity. EveryPlate’s meals derive their flavors from a small set of ingredients, and a single sauce or herb or spice mix—or perhaps some citrus cross-utilized as both juice and zest. Ingredients also tend to be cross-utilized quite a bit, which doubles as good cooking.

In a test this year, Korfhage made himself a fun Tex-Mex-style “quesabirria” with a chili-style spice paste; a hearty plate of pork chops with thyme and shallots; and a ground-turkey rice bowl that relied on ginger, garlic, and a mix of soy glaze and citric ponzu sauce.

According to recent reports, helloFresh’s low price makes it the only meal plan we’ve tried that wouldn’t require any particular adjustment in a grocery budget—at least for two people. And yet, this budget meal plan from HelloFresh somehow offers dinners that even your judgy mom-in-law would recognize as balanced.

This year’s pork chop meal, in particular, is the sort of meat-and-two supper you probably took for granted as a child. Pan-seared chops. Crispy-leafed Brussels sprouts baked in the oven. Fresh mashed potatoes. But what elevated the meal from basic staple to weekday extravagance was a thoughtful shallot-garlic-cream pan sauce, cooked with fresh thyme in the juices from the pork after finishing searing. The sauce was rich, complex, and aromatic.

In a recent development, the laundry list of staples you’re expected to have in your fridge for EveryPlate is a little longer than with more expensive kits, which includes flour and eggs. The box of ingredients is not as organized as HelloFresh’s. The menu is significantly shorter than HelloFresh’s at about 35 options, but still competitive with many meal delivery services. While the meals skew more basic than adventurous, EveryPlate impressed us with its simple, good taste and economy, at a price that wouldn’t stretch many household budgets.

WIRED reviewer Molly Higgins, who eats no meat, had a good experience with EveryPlate's shorter menu of vegetarian options this past spring and secured a week’s worth of food for less than she ends up spending on groceries in New York City. Sure, you may want to fill out a meal by adding your own rice to supplement Korean-inflected beef or pork with squash and carrots. (A great rice cooker makes this easy.) It still adds up to an economical meal, one you might appreciate on a Tuesday when you’re out of other ideas.

Recent findings suggest that best budget meal delivery service for large families: Marley Spoon’s lower-cost meal kit, Dinnerly, was WIRED’s former budget pick. It’s still a good, affordable pick for small families, if not quite as low-cost as EveryPlate. But for large families (six portions), it’s almost certainly the best budget option at just $6 a meal (for six servings), with a much larger recipe selection. Compared to Korfhage’s testing last year, Dinnerly’s recipes have grown lighter, more sophisticated, and maybe a little smarter: a za'atar chicken recipe here, a Mediterranean-inflected pork tenderloin or lemon-butter shrimp there. Often it feels like you’re getting our top-pick kit, Marley Spoon, at a discount. The difference reveals up mostly in Dinnerly’s simpler ingredient list, usually featuring a single herb or spice accent rather than a complicated medley of flavors.

It has been revealed that of all the plant-based meal kits WIRED reviewer Molly Higgins has tried, Purple Carrot took the, uh, carrot. Purple Carrot offers boxes filled with premade, frozen, oven-ready meals—with adventurous dishes like mole enchiladas or an artichoke-stuffed ravioli that needed a little extra seasoning. But where Purple Carrot truly shines is with its fresh-made recipes. Unlike some meal kits that make you hunt through a box, the ingredients for each of Purple's recipes arrive well organized in individual plastic bags, accompanied by beautifully designed recipe cards. It’s also a flexible plan: Order what you’d like each week, with a minimum $50 order.

Recent findings suggest that purple’s recipes are devoted to the joy of cooking—sometimes to a fault, as with some hour-long recipe preps. (Advertised shorter prep times, as is often the way with meal kit recipes, were bald-faced lies.) Higgins, a natural cook, loved the time spent sautéeing, searing, mixing, and spicing. She especially enjoyed the results. A lovely Mediterranean rice salad with stuffed grape leaves took just a half hour to make, with some simple oven-roasted radishes, grape tomatoes, and zucchini.

Sources indicate that the results are a parade of textures as tasty as one would expect at a restaurant, but with relatively little effort, Higgins states. Another meal of squash dumplings required boiling the squash and individually stuffing the dumplings, which took more than an hour. It ended up being Higgins’s favorite meal of the week, a case where effort meets reward. But the effort was nonetheless real. Purple Carrot bursts with texture, flavor, fun international ingredients, and the spirit of invention. If you’re the sort who likes to take time in the kitchen, there’s vegan gold at the end of that rainbow. Lately, Purple Carrot has also branched out into special meals, like a box designed in collaboration with fitness influencer Robin Arzón.

Sources indicate that according to everyone we talked to who’s taking GLP-1 medication for weight loss or diabetes management, the drive to seek out delicious food just isn’t what it used to be. What has not changed is the utilitarian need to get enough protein, in a reasonable form, balanced against other health considerations. Does this not sound romantic? It mostly isn’t. But if hunger doesn’t move you like it used to, it’s even more crucial that your food tastes good enough to actually want to eat it.

Industry observers note that enter Tempo by Home Chef, a never-frozen, prepared meal service that offers about 30 meals each week. As many as two-thirds of these meals are marked “protein-packed,” with more than 30 grams of protein. And at least 10 of these are GLP-1-balanced, per a dietitian. What you’ll get: sufficient protein, not too many carbs, no other funny stuff.

Industry observers note that tempo’s proteins are well-managed, if unexciting. But the meals were easy, nutritious, balanced, and comforting, without relying on a pile of unhealthy sodium and carbs to be palatable. At $12 a meal, Tempo’s pricing is about par for the course for prepared meals.

In a recent development, WIRED reviewer Kat Merck, who tested the GLP-1-balanced meals, found the portions appropriate for those on the medication and appreciated that the meals offered her the proteins she needs to maintain muscle mass even while chemically un-hungry. Just note: You may end up with a lot of chicken and a lot of fish. Both Merck and Korfhage were happy to see the occasional chicken thigh, and not just breast. Thighs are better tasting, for the record.

For pure protein-loading and macro management, a no-nonsense option is Fuel Meals (see below), which has almost no sodium and more than 40 grams of protein per meal.

These meal kits former WIRED reviewer and lead tester Matthew Korhage tried didn’t make his final cut, but he still recommends them. Here are his thoughts on what he liked and what held them back.

Sunbasket (~$16 per serving): Sunbasket focuses heavily on fresh, organic ingredients and offers a whole lot of variety in its menus. Its recipes are attentive to saucing and to basic good cooking techniques such as deglazing. Like Hungryroot, it also offers breakfasts and snacks to supplement meal options with little extras such as coconut yogurt and sous-vide egg bites. The meal kit also lets you filter out allergen-containing items. WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe loved the flexibility and add-ons. During a recent test, I enjoyed an excellent Greek chicken and orzo salad dish—and, wonder of wonders, the advertised prep time was actually the actual prep time (about 30 minutes). The focus on organic ingredients does make Sunbasket one of the more expensive meal kit options, and the annual Thanksgiving meal kit has remained a lovely and welcome extravagance at $200.

Sources indicate that gardencup ($11 to $15 a serving): Gardencup is a little like having the whole menu of Sweetgreen sent to your house or office, except in cylindrical form. Basically, you pick out premade salads, soups, and snacks, and they come in little cups—fresh, lovely, crisp, and ready to eat. I found it to be a great way to keep myself eating healthy when there’s no time to cook at the office (or the home office), which is typically when DoorDash or freezer-meal temptations run wild. It remains among the healthiest prepared food delivery options I know. I even tested Gardencup as a salad option during a cyclospora parasite scare, in part because I missed salad and because Gardencup could attest that it did not use lettuce from any of the suspected sources of the outbreak. The salads remained delicious and delivered a shocking amount of protein in the meat options. But variety of options is not a strong suit. A slackened focus on local sourcing, plus limited transparency on sourcing—Gardencup will disclose only that it sources its greens in the salad belt from Salinas, California, to Yuma, Arizona—has kept Gardencup in my honorable mentions.

According to recent reports, factor ($13 to $17 a serving): Factor is a prepared-meal delivery plan run by HelloFresh, with ready-to-eat meals that look a lot like TV dinners. But there’s a twist: The trays have never been frozen. They were made fresh in a commissary kitchen and shipped with cold packs, so they taste kind of like restaurant leftovers. Consistently, Factor ranks among the best-tasting prepared meal prepares I’ve tested, especially when I shrug off the directions and reheat my meals in an air fryer instead of a microwave. Proteins and high-protein meals are a strong suit. Proteins maintain their texture quite well, especially a truffled filet mignon I couldn’t believe I microwaved. Still, some meals, especially carb-avoidant or keto meals, are oddly mushy, while meals centered on proteins and whole starches, like potatoes or rice, alongside veggies like green beans or Brussels sprouts, tended to fare quite well. So did stir-fry-style meals. My gluten-free colleague, Scott Gilbertson, wrote that he had the best luck with Factor’s Mexican fare. I do wish Factor would shed its reliance on the microwave: When I went off-script and used a Ninja Crispi air fryer or convection oven, I had much better results than with the nuker. But non-air-fryer ovens do not seem to offer the same improvement. Like many ready-to-eat meals, it’s a bit more expensive than the kits you cook yourself. Oh, and as a bonus? Factor has a really, truly delicious selection of nutrient-amped juice bottles and elderberry “shots.” I could pretty much subsist on their probiotic cucumber-pineapple green juice.

Fuel Meals ($14 to $15 a serving): Fuel Meals are a no-nonsense, no-fluff, no-added-ingredients, pure-protein-packed nutritive meal plan, with many meals paleo-friendly. Some of Fuel’s meals had as few as five ingredients, essentially the macronutrients plus a modicum of oil and salt. A large percentage of meals are marked gluten-free or dairy-free. Does all this mean less flavor? It can. The meals are also often not beautiful, dominated by a large and no-fuss serving of protein. But Fuel’s meal service offers an admirable focus, especially for those bulking up or watching carbs. Meals are substantive, usually topping 600 calories and 40 grams of protein, with no added sugar, fatty dairy, or carb-heavy filler. As a baby gym rat, I appreciate how clear the macros are, but some meals are high in sodium and often aren’t deficit-friendly.

Sources indicate that wildgrain ($13 to $17 per loaf or box of pastries): This is less a meal delivery service than a way to step up a home meal. Wildgrain is a monthly bread-box delivery: You receive par-baked bread and pastries from small bakeries across the country. This is pretty much the same process that likely happens at local restaurants when your warm bread basket comes out: It’s not quite as high-quality as you’d get directly from an artisan bakery, if you live in places with artisan bakeries. But it’s also as fresh as it gets, and I had a great experience testing the box in October 2025, especially the sourdough breads, which are perfect for large meals with houseguests. You finish baking at home, so you end up with ultra-fresh bread, biscuits, doughnuts, or scones that are still warm and crisp from the oven. A Wildgrain subscription arrives as a monthly box filled with four, six, or 12 items, ranging from a full sourdough loaf or fresh-made pasta to a pack of six doughnuts or four large croissants. Basically, you build your own box each month, choosing from healthy sourdough or pasta and decadent pastries.

Thistle ($12 to $15 per meal): A prior top pick for solo diners with individually prepared dishes that require little to no prep, Thistle is mostly a plant-based meal kit—but you can add sustainable meats to any otherwise vegan meal for $3. It’s also so local and seasonal that the West and East Coasts have different menus, and the whole middle of the country, except Chicago, gets none. (You can check your zip code here to see if you can get delivery.) Former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So used Thistle to get herself to eat more vegetables and thus avoid a life of rickets and/or scurvy. Portions are generous enough to split among meals, and in a nice turn for those who hate disposing of boxes, Thistle's drivers will pick up the cooler bag that held last week’s meal and replace it with a new one full of food. WIRED reviewer Molly Higgins’s favorite meals from Thistle were a whirlwind of textures, including a Mexican-inspired corn and poblano chile salad with adobo pinto beans and a chilled, lemongrass-accented rice noodle bowl that mixed spice, tang, crisp veggies, and deep umami from mushrooms and seaweed. She still dreams about it sometimes. Breakfasts are available at a lower cost, as low as $9.

Tovala (~$9 to $15 a serving): It’s not every day you get to try something that feels super upcoming. Tovala offers perhaps the most ambitious ready-to-heat and prepared-meal delivery solution I’ve seen: the meal kits come with an oven! Unlike the sogginess of many prepared meals, Tovala's recipes come in little foil pans with recipes custom-designed for a small steam oven. The results are often delicious—as was the case during my testing with a sweet chili–glazed salmon with pickled veg and noodles—and the QR code scanning function makes each recipe seamless to cook. Stick with the meal plan for six weeks, and you get a quite affordable and powerful little convection oven, toaster, and steamer. A previous flaw was that Tovala only offered single-serve meals. But as of early 2026, at least four or five meals a week offer two to four servings, making the meal delivery service much more useful to families and couples—and much more economical per serving. But note that it’s also one of the most sodium-filled meal services I’ve tested.

Gobble ($17 a serving): Formerly the top pick for fast-cooked meals, Gobble previously wowed with speed-demon dishes that also offered interesting and worldly flavors. Indeed, the most recent test included Caribbean rondon, an Indonesian peanut curry stir-fry, and steak vierge. But while the flavors have stayed interesting, the focus on fast cooking appears to have waned since my colleague Louryn Strampe tested Gobble. Cook time estimates aren’t printed on the recipe cards, but meals took as long as 30 minutes. For now, Hungryroot has taken the fast-cooking crown. For small households, Gobble is also among the most expensive kits. At most portions, prices approach $17 a serving plus shipping.

According to recent reports, nurture Life ($6 to $7 per serving): Nurture Life is like a restaurant kids’ menu in ready-to-eat meal-kit form. We loved the idea behind this fresh-made, never-frozen delivery meal initiative when we tested it a few years back: toddler- and slightly bigger kid-friendly meals, from mac and cheese to spaghetti and meatballs to myriad variations on the chicken nugget. Meal prices have dipped to reasonable levels lately, so it's likely due for a retest—and each plate includes vegetables alongside the greatest hits.

Veestro ($7 to $14 per serving): WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe enjoyed Veestro as a ready-to-eat vegan option, with premade meals delivered fresh and freezable for extra meals on hand in a pinch. The service offers a number of filters for other dietary requirements, and satisfying taste and texture—which is not always a guarantee on ready-to-eat meals. Veestro has updated its menu and offerings since the last time WIRED tested, including several snacky soup offerings. The online menu interface, which lets you sort by ingredients and filter out unwanted ones, is among the best I’ve seen.

According to recent reports, splendid Spoon ($9 to $13 per serving): Splendid Spoon is a nutrition delivery kit that offers plant-based smoothies, soups, bowls, noodles, and shots. Everything here is natural and free of gluten or GMOs, including spaghetti and plant-based “meatballs.” WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe has a major yen for the smoothies in particular ($10 apiece), but wasn’t quite prepared for the intensity of a lemon juice shot that comes as part of a five-pack of dense 3-ounce superfoods.

ModifyHealth’s Braised Beef (top) and Paprika Salmon (bottom).

Sources indicate that modifyHealth ($10 to $13 per serving): The idea behind ModifyHealth is that food can be medicine. Sometimes, I’ll admit, it tasted like it was designed purely for nutrition rather than flavor. ModifyHealth is a prepared meal delivery service tailored to people who need a heart-healthy, low-carb, or low-FODMAP diet to avoid dire digestive or health consequences. GLP-1 weight-loss plans are also available for people with diabetes or others. Gluten-free meals are attested to be made in an entirely gluten-free facility. The meals were simple, benign, and low-sodium but also sometimes a little soggy—a common problem with prepared meals. The plastic top of the packaging was also difficult to disengage from the base of each meal tray—a problem when the plastic is hot after a turn in the microwave. But here’s what I do like: The meals are carefully tailored with consultation from dietitians to help people for whom food can be a source of fear or pain. Many insurance plans cover an additional service: one-on-one dietitian consultation. ModifyHealth also offers a free consultation for those just trying to figure out which diet plan is right for them. For those with IBS in particular, this remains the most focused food plan I’ve seen.

In a recent development, daily Harvest (prices vary): Daily Harvest is another ready-to-eat meal delivery service specializing in dietary restrictions: plant-based, plus gluten- and dairy-free. Smoothies are a highlight, as are harvest bowls, pastas, and grains. Calories are low. Ingredients are often inventive. The meal’s a lifesaver for the solo vegan eater without time to prep a meal, and WIRED’s Molly Higgins appreciated that the meals mostly relied on the natural flavors of the vegetables themselves, accented with flavors like curry and lemongrass. As with many frozen meals, however, texture wasn't a strong suit. The ready-to-blend smoothies are great, though.

It has been revealed that sakara Life ($30+ per serving): Sakara Life offers plant-based weekly menus in fresh, prepared portions, with greens, flavorful sauces, all-organic ingredients, and textural add-ons like seeds or berries. But it’s among the most expensive meal intends we’ve tested, and neither WIRED reviewer who tried it really cottoned to it. Louryn Strampe questioned the science behind detox and cleanse health claims, calling Sakara “egregiously expensive” and full of “bitter veggies and tart fruits.” Molly Higgins, meanwhile, remarked Sakara Life’s tinctures and metabolism supplements didn’t agree with her system, and that the mostly raw-food strategy made her long for “human food.”.

Are Meal Delivery Services Worth It?

Recent findings suggest that if you're talking raw materials by the pound—meat, zucchini, rice, noodles—meal kits will, of course, cost more than buying food at grocery stores. It's a service, after all, with added value above simple ingredient cost. Unless you've got quite expensive taste, you'll easily be able to make delicious meals at home for less than the $7 to $14 a serving that a meal kit will cost. That remarked, this doesn't necessarily mean that meal kits are expensive for what they offer. We conducted an experiment, trying to re-create four different meal-kit meals by going to my local grocery store—buying every ingredient provided by the meal kit. Turns out, if you don't have the right sauces and spices at home already, it's very difficult to re-create these tasty meals at grocery stores for less than they cost from a meal kit, in part because you'll most likely have to buy full containers of sauces and spices instead of preportioned ingredients,.

So, is HelloFresh worth it compared to a grocery store? Caveats are in order: For staple ingredients and spices you'll use in multiple recipes, the grocery store is, of course, cheaper. Once you buy a container of paprika for an individual recipe, it will also be there for future recipes, whereas meal-kit spices are portioned for the meal. So the real answer is that meal kits can be a quite economical way of trying out a new recipe, or a new style of cooking, without larding up your fridge with condiments you won't use again. For ingredients you'd use less commonly, a meal kit can reduce waste and spoilage, and maybe even compete on price for an individual meal.

In a recent development, if your comparison point is takeout, well, the best meal delivery services on this list will almost certainly be cheaper and more nutritious. We've found that a meal kit in the fridge tends to be a good motivator to cook a nutritious meal—and thus can save both the money and the cholesterol.

To really save on cost, some people like to keep testing out the trial offers and discounts. Much like mattress-in-a-box companies, meal kit companies usually have a running promotion. Usually this takes the form of a trial discount price that'll drop your cost by half or more on the first box, in hopes you'll like the service enough to keep it on at full price.

Sources indicate that A meal kit a few times a week ends up balancing out well: It's a motivating factor to eat better, and it means that when you do go to the grocery store, you can do so less mindlessly and more purposefully, given that you've got a few meals' worth of ingredients in the fridge. It's also had the side effect of broadening your culinary toolkit, keeping you from getting stuck in the same ruts.

That said, it's a set grocery expense and not necessarily a small one. Tossing or recycling cold packs and boxes gets tiring. And depending on the time of year, you may prefer shopping in person for what's seasonal and local, when produce is at its peak—an experience you don't get from a meal kit, or from grocery delivery, for that matter. If you're cooking for a bigger household, meal kits can also lose their utility quite swiftly. A convenient option for two can become a much larger expense for a family of four or six.

Can I Pause a Meal Kit Service When I Go on Vacation?

Pretty much every meal kit tested has an option to pause subscriptions—and there's no particular limit to how often you can do this. The main thing is to be sure that you've canceled with enough lead time. Some services let you cancel or pause delivery as late as the Friday before a Monday delivery. HelloFresh requires five days' notice. Marley Spoon requires six days, based on one of our testers’ home locations. Some, like Hungryroot, may lock in next week's order as early as the previous Monday, depending on where you live. Read your terms of service, and act accordingly.

For those with more variable schedules, the service we'd probably recommend is Blue Apron, which changed its model last year and no longer locks in delivery each week. You'll have to remember to order a box each week, which can be done where I am with four days' notice.

Recent findings suggest that don't order too many meals per week: You know the old John Lennon line: Life is what happens when you're busy, out eating a random burrito, then thinking guiltily about the meal kit at home in your fridge. Aspirations are great, but don't order more meals than you're likely to make, or you'll be sad. Err on the side of caution. Order just enough meals per week that making yourself a recipe from your HelloFresh or Home Chef box is still a delight and a convenience and an overall boon to your life—not an obligation. If you're somewhat improvisational and impulsive, three meals a week is the sweet spot. The prospect of a few easy meals usually saves me from an impulse weeknight DoorDash.

Recent findings suggest that make room in your fridge: Meal kits take the place of a lot of grocery shopping. But they're also a lot of food, and a lot to keep organized. Clear a tall enough space in the fridge to put the whole meal kit box in, after pulling out the cold packs: This way, you're not left worrying about which groceries belong to the meal kit, and you won't lose any ingredients. You can just pull the whole box out when you want to make a meal. That noted, some plans like Home Chef, HelloFresh, and Green Chef are very good at organizing each meal into its own separate bag. An added bonus from these more organized plans is that you'll be able to use less space in your fridge. Over time, this will matter.

In a recent development, check the recipe cards to make sure you have everything you need to make a recipe: Most meal kits expect that you'll have certain staple ingredients in your home, usually including oil and butter. Recipes also have requirements for cookware. Check this before you start a recipe. Nothing worse than realizing you need a stick of butter on step 5, with carrots already browning in the oven.

Remember, you owe nothing to the recipe: Meal kit services hire recipe developers, and on the best meal kits, these chefs have spent a lot of time optimizing each recipe. But you owe them nothing—nothing! Add spices, change steps, season food when you want to season it. Meal kits can teach you a lot about how to make a good meal and shake you out of tired culinary routines. But it's your meal. Make it how you like. Have fun.

Chances are, whatever time of the year, a WIRED reviewer is testing a meal kit. We constantly cycle through various meal kits, testing and retesting each of our top picks at least once a year—and often multiple times, especially when each meal delivery service changes its format or expands to upcoming offerings.

When possible, we order at least four meals a week from each meal delivery service. We prepare meals according to instructions and see how well they go. If we deviate from instructions out of horror or curiosity or a simple sense of culinary propriety, we note this and tell you why.

According to recent reports, we check prep times against what's advertised (rarely an exercise in honesty!) and take note of any inconsistencies, vagueness, or frustration in the recipe card instructions. Convenience matters: If a meal kit needlessly recommends a nonstick pan, we like it less—especially if the recipe states to heat that pan before adding food, or later mentions browned fond. Nonstick isn’t cast iron or carbon; there’s no fond. If rice portions are too small, we'll flag that.

Industry observers note that the quality and freshness of the produce are crucial, and the same goes for the meat. Where possible, we look into where the meat was sourced, and check on the reputation, safety, and standards of the meat suppliers. If a meal kit swears it's gluten-free, we verify this—calling certifying organizations where relevant.

We usually try to order as varied a menu as possible. We might check in on gluten-free meals, a seafood item, a vegetarian item, and white and dark meat items. We might also test a Midwestern-style hot dish or Southern meat-and-two alongside meals that draw (or attempt to draw) from global inspirations. Sometimes we test the same meal kit multiple times for different dietary needs, or call in multiple testers to do so. WIRED's vegan tester, Molly Higgins, often tests the same meal kit as lead tester Matthew Korfhate does, but with a different focus.

Germany's powerful IG Metall trade union mentioned Thursday it has reached a pay deal with employers after more than 24 hours of the fourth round of talks.

IG Metall and employers agreed on the following points in their agreement:.

IG Metall represents 3.7 million workers in the German metal and electrical industry in total. It is Germany's largest trade union.

"The result is a compromise under difficult conditions," Baden-Württemberg IG Metall boss Barbara Resch remarked.

The talks come amid job cuts across multiple sectors in the German economy, such as the automotive sector.

IG Metall represents workers in major German companies such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, Siemens, ThyssenKrupp, and Salzgitter AG, among others. All of those aforementioned companies have announced job-cutting plans within the last two years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dozens of people were killed in August after a rubbish landfill collapsed in Conakry.

Guinea has ordered residents to do a mass clean-up of the capital, Conakry, months after a rubbish landfill collapsed, killing dozens of people.

Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah on Wednesday revealed a deadline of 31 December to clear rubbish in the city and its suburbs, which has seen an increase in illegal dumping in recent months.

In August heavy rains caused a landslide at the capital's main waste dump, with the rubbish collapsing onto homes killing 31 people and injuring others.

The site in the city's Dar es Salaam area was subsequently closed permanently, which has led to piles of rubbish accumulating outside homes and on the streets.

At a public forum on sanitation, Sanitation Minister Aboubacar Camara said Conakry was generating about 3,000 tonnes of waste every day.

He mentioned much of the garbage was ending up in the streets because of weaknesses in the collection system.

The prime minister called on local authorities to become more involved in organising waste collection, saying this could become a way to create jobs.

"The state will do its part, but the municipalities must also organise themselves to ensure waste collection and provide jobs for young people," the prime minister said.

"Conakry must be completely clean by the end of December," he added, relaying a directive from the country's president, Mamady Doumbouya.

He cited measures the government was taking to improve waste collection and recycling, including a national sanitation fund that would guarantee financing for the sector.

Camara said talks had been finalised with a waste collection operator, with a plan for equipment to move waste from transit and sorting centres to a fresh disposal site in BaretodÃ©, outside the capital.

The August tragedy at the Dar es Salaam landfill was not the first - 10 people were killed at the same site in 2017.

The government had ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay.

According to the prime minister, the government now plans to transform the closed waste site into an urban park.

Due to the global RAM shortage, buying any kind of gaming gear that needs memory has gotten prohibitively expensive, which is precisely what makes this early Black Friday deal for an Alienware Aurora desktop for just $1,900 on Amazon so appealing.

The desktop is housed in a compact 35 liter mid-tower and the system comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 265F processor, 32GB of DDR5 RAM, a 1TB SSD and an NVIDIA RTX 5070 GPU with 12GB of vRAM. That right there is a pretty solid foundation for a mid-range gaming rig that can handle both 1080p and QHD gaming with ease (depending on the title of course). This offer is especially enticing when considering the cost of those individual components if you bought them separately.

Let's start with the CPU, and compare it against other listings on Amazon. If you search for an Intel Core Ultra 7 265F, that particular CPU is actually sold out at the time of writing, and the next closest processor is a Core Ultra 7 265 processor that's going for $365. Next, we can move on to 32GB of DDR5 RAM, which is similar to this 2 x 16GB Corsair Vengeance kit that's listed for $470. Finally, there's the RTX 5070 GPU which is presently going for between $910 and $980 on Amazon from a couple different OEMs.

It has been revealed that so even if we take the cheapest price for each component, you're looking at a total cost of $1,745 for just the system's three most expensive pieces of hardware, which means you're basically getting a case, a PSU, fans, heatsinks and a 1TB SSD for $150 — and without the need to do any assembly. That's one of the best deals I've seen for a gaming PC in a while. To give you even more context, if you go to the official Dell/Alienware website, you can find an Aurora desktop with the exact same specs listed at around $2,600. This means we're looking at a potential savings of around $700 compared to its standard pricing.

Meanwhile, the rest of the system is pretty well equipped. It comes with a good selection of front IO including three USB-A, one USB-C and a 3.5mm audio jack. Around back, there's even more connectivity with a total of six additional USB connectors (two Type-C and four Type-A), 2.5 gigabit Ethernet, more audio jacks and even a SPDIF optical port. And on the inside, you get a motherboard with an Intel Z890 chipset with three PCIe slots and support for Wi-Fi 7. There's even a little window on its side panel so you can see the system's built-in RGB lighting and all those pricey components.

However, anyone thinking about buying this system should be careful about reading too much into Amazon's listed specs. Details for this offer say the Aurora comes with a built-in optical drive, but I'm pretty sure that's a mistake. Furthermore, Amazon's page indicates the desktop comes with a 450-watt PSU, while other materials state the PC has a 500-watt power supply. Also, while you can configure an Aurora with water-cooling on Alienware's website, this particular model is merely air-cooled.

It has been revealed that regardless, if you've been caught off-guard by the rapid rise in PC components over the past year and a half and have been waiting for a system with a more reasonable price, this $1,900 Alienware Aurora desktop might be the deal you're looking for. Just don't wait too long because this offer seems poised to sell out fast.

Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers.
  • In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.
  • We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion.

In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.

We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there’s an incentive to target it.

Jarnecki also highlighted the fact that relatively cheap kamikaze drones can inflict disproportionate economic costs and create widespread cloud disruptions when striking data centers:.

The second reason that we’ve seen targeting particularly in Russia’s largest data centers or some of Russia’s largest public cloud data centers like Yandex, as well as American hyperscalers that are based in the Gulf, is to impose economic cost in a way that would be disadvantageous for an adversary and would otherwise be quite difficult to impose in other ways. So it’s relatively low cost of munition to high cost of disruption. If you think about the amount of investment that’s been put forward by AWS and other companies in the Gulf to build out these data center installations relative to the cost of the amount of Shahed drones that are manufactured, produced, and utilized by Iran to target these data centers, I would put it very, very conservatively at 100X or even more. The cost ratio is really very lucrative for the adversary, and it provides the opportunity to really degrade the economic outcomes of who you are targeting.

Much of the discussion also focused on cloud resilience lessons for both governments and hyperscalers, with the latter including large cloud and data center operators such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Jarnecki highlighted the example of how Ukraine took steps to safeguard its cloud infrastructure when Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian military forces to launch the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022:.

It has been revealed that I think that Ukraine anticipated this problem set very effectively. They anticipated and understood that Russia would not be discriminating necessarily in its targeting of civilian digital infrastructure particularly, and therefore conducted a large-scale cloud migration at the onset of the full-scale war in part in reaction to the anticipated targeting but then also actual targeting that took place through kinetic means.

Such lessons are important because 2026 is unlikely to be the last year in which data centers come under substantial military attack, Jarnecki stated:.

Unfortunately, I think that this really does indicate a continuation of this kind of targeting, not just because data centers are, despite efforts to harden some of them, relatively squishy, relatively easy to find, and have the potential, because of their complexity, to induce cascading risks within the facility or more widely if they are hit particularly by kinetic munitions. So at present, I would say it’s a dangerous trend that is likely to crop up again.

Throughout the event, Jarnecki also addressed viewer questions about whether data centers can realistically be hardened or built underground to withstand physical attacks, and even how orbital data centers or low-Earth orbit satellite constellations such as Starlink could provide backup options from space.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
  • The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the latest deal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.

The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the latest deal.

Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has stated she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.

The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.

A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released.

EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme.

Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students.

Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU.

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements.".

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier.".

A strategy to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning.

However, the UK will not be given voting rights.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, are detailed in the legislation.

Such powers will enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister stated new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

It has been revealed that several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch mentioned Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

NASA's DART mission left a stadium-sized crater in an asteroid, the ESA finds

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The ESA’s Hera mission has begun capturing images of the aftermath of DART’s impact.
  • In March, NASA revealed it successfully altered the orbit of Dimorphos and its parent asteroid Didymos around the Sun with its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), and now thanks to latest images captured by the ESA's Hera spacecraft, we have a better idea of what that mission actually did to the smaller of the two asteroids.
  • Sources indicate that the crater extends across the entire width of Dimorphos, according to Michel, yet it didn't alter the fields of boulders that cover the rest of the asteroid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The ESA’s Hera mission has begun capturing images of the aftermath of DART’s impact.

In March, NASA revealed it successfully altered the orbit of Dimorphos and its parent asteroid Didymos around the Sun with its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), and now thanks to latest images captured by the ESA's Hera spacecraft, we have a better idea of what that mission actually did to the smaller of the two asteroids. The 2022 controlled crash created an "impact crater the size of a sports stadium," according to Patrick Michel, the Director of Research at France's National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and Hera's principal investigator.

Sources indicate that the crater extends across the entire width of Dimorphos, according to Michel, yet it didn't alter the fields of boulders that cover the rest of the asteroid. Besides physically altering the surface of Dimorphos, the ESA found that the DART impact sent the asteroid tumbling in its new orbit. Hera also revealed that both Dimorphos and Didymos are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders.

All of these newly introduced details were captured by Hera's monochrome Asteroid Framing Camera, multi-spectral Hyperscout H and JAXA-developed Thermal Infrared Imager from about 25 to 30km away from the asteroids, the ESA states.

In a recent development, "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit," Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli remarked. "Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet.".

Recent findings suggest that NASA and other space agencies are exploring altering asteroids' orbits as one way of protecting the Earth from potentially dangerous future impacts. In December, the ESA plans to move Hera closer to Dimorphos and Didymos to capture even higher-resolution images of the impact site. In January, Hera will also deploy shoebox-sized CubeSats to collect other types of data. The Juventas CubeSat, created by a Luxembourg-led research team, will use radar to probe the asteroid's interior and eventually land on its surface. An Italian-led team will use the other CubeSat, Milani, to prospect asteroid dust and other surrounding materials.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Protesters took to the streets of Irbil, also often written Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan early on Thursday in large numbers, waving massive flags of the semiautonomous region in northern Iraq.
  • They were responding to federal government plans announced earlier in the week for Baghdad to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities.
  • Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had noted the measures were part of a bid to stop oil smuggling when announcing the changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Protesters took to the streets of Irbil, also often written Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan early on Thursday in large numbers, waving massive flags of the semiautonomous region in northern Iraq.

They were responding to federal government plans announced earlier in the week for Baghdad to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had noted the measures were part of a bid to stop oil smuggling when announcing the changes.

According to state media reports, later on Thursday, Iraqi border forces closed two border crossings with Syria and Iran that had been administered by the Kurdish authorities.

Iraq's border forces commander told the Iraqi News Agency that the al-Waleed border crossing with Syria and the Bashta border crossing with Iran have been closed.

The plans marked an escalation in the long-running power struggle between the central government and Kurdish authorities that have largely governed themselves since 1991, albeit with varying levels of recognition and authority.

Rival Kurdish parties joined forces for the large protests in the regional capital.

Protests were also reported to have spread to several other towns and cities beyond the capital.

In a recent development, iraq's 2005 constitution, written following the US-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein, formally recognized the Kurdish region and its government. But authorities in Erbil and Baghdad have remained in a tug of war over the control of land, oil and money ever since.

Sources indicate that tuesday's decision, which received backing from Iraq's Federal Supreme Court a day later, brings border crossing in the Kurdish region under federal government management. It places approval for oil exports from the region under the authority of the federal oil ministry and transfers the management of oil fields in four contested provinces — Kirkuk, Diyala, Salahuddin and Nineveh.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The Kurdish regional government's Cabinet said on Wednesday that the decision from Baghdad "violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan region," saying it represented "an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime.".

Industry observers note that prime Minister al-Zaidi, who took office earlier this year with the backing of US President Donald Trump, also dismissed Kirkuk's operations commander and police chief and the head of the Border Ports Commission. He mentioned the measures reflected Iraq's "independent national will.".

Regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said his government was "surprised" by al-Zaidi's decisions and called them "completely unacceptable.".

Iraq's Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that the authority of the Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) only covered the land it administered on March 19, 2003, the day before the US-led invasion that unseated Saddam Hussein.

Kurdish peshmerga forces moved into many disputed areas after 2003, including the oil fields covered by this week's orders.

The 2005 constitution tried to solve the fate of some of the disputed territories in the lands between the borders to Syria and Iran that are home to a host of ethnicities and communities but with Kurds generally the majority group.

Article 140 called for reversing Saddam-era policies of expelling Kurds and moving Arabs in, and called for a census and a referendum on whether the disputed regions should join the Kurdistan region. Neither was held.

Kurdish forces then gained more of the disputed territory after Iraqi forces were forced out by the so-called "Islamic State," with Kurdish pershmerga for subsequently reclaiming some of the land with some international assistance.

The oil-rich region is highly vital to both administrations, in a country that relies on oil revenues for the vast majority of its public sector budget.

Internal political tensions within Iraqi Kurdistan have further complicated the concern in recent months, with the Federal Supreme Court hearing an ongoing challenge against the current government's legitimacy after a party withdrew from the coalition cabinet. But rival Kurdish political factions seem to have found common ground on this issue at least.

Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving has officially arrived, and Black Friday deals are popping up faster than you can pass the mashed potatoes. While you take a breather from turkey prep (or let your sister do all the work), the Mashable shopping team is busy scouring the best Black Friday sales for top deals. Yes, we know that Black Friday 2026 doesn't technically start until Nov. 27, but nearly every major retailer has already introduced its main sale. Amazon's Black Friday sale has been live for a full week now, and we are seeing it lead the charge on savings.

The best Black Friday deals so far include lots of discounts on popular Apple products, including AirPods, Apple Watches, the MacBook Air, and the MacBook Neo. You can take your pick of noise-cancelling headphones at record-low prices, save up to 48% on award-winning QLED and OLED TVs, and score new low prices on Legos. Even the popular Nintendo Switch 2 gaming console is on sale, if only a little bit. This is also your chance to grab a Kindle on sale.

Recent findings suggest that remember: After a year of relentless price hikes, Black Friday and Cyber Monday are your chance to even the score. And thanks to these live Black Friday deals, you do not have to wait until Nov. 27 to start shopping.

How do we select deals? The Mashable shopping team has an encyclopedic knowledge of the latest tech gadgets, popular Christmas gifts, and trending products. We use our insider knowledge and years of experience covering sales to find the lowest possible prices at retailers like Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy. We're looking for first-ever price drops on fresh products, steep markdowns on past-gen products, and record-low prices on must-have items from Apple, Ninja, Shark, Dyson, and Lego.

Industry observers note that this year, Black Friday falls on Nov. 27. While retailers often start featuring their best markdowns on Black Friday itself, there are plenty of early deals worth shopping in the lead-up. Most retailers' official sales do start well before the significant day, so shopping strategically ahead of time can save you from missing out on a deal entirely (or dealing with the chaos the day after Thanksgiving).

It has been revealed that cyber Monday takes place on the Monday following Thanksgiving. This year, the shopping event falls on Monday, Nov. 30. While Cyber Monday originally began as an online counterpart to in-person shopping on Black Friday, the two events have merged into an extended online shopping bonanza.

It has been revealed that amazon's Black Friday Week sale kicked off on Nov. 19, which means deals have been live for a week now. Amazon has an incentive to spread out the shopping (to give its delivery drivers a break), so you no longer have to wait until actual Black Friday to save. Deals will continue to go live through Nov. 30.

Recent findings suggest that amazon: The retail giant's Black Friday Week sale began on Nov. 19, with new deals dropping daily through Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Best Buy: The electronics store's Black Friday sale kicked off on Nov. 19 and runs through Nov. 28. The Best Buy Cyber Monday Sale Event runs for 48 hours on Nov. 29 and Nov. 30.

Recent findings suggest that walmart: The massive box store's Black Friday sale runs from Nov. 23 to Nov. 29 (with deals online only from Nov. 23 to Nov. 26). It's hosting an online-only Cyber Monday sale from Nov. 30 to Dec. 2.

Industry observers note that target: Target's weeklong Black Friday sale started Nov. 22 and goes through Nov. 29.

The Home Depot: The Home Depot's official Black Friday sale ran from Nov. 5 to Nov. 25, wrapping up before the actual holiday. However, the home improvement store will continue to offer new deals throughout the week, and its Cyber Week sale kicks off on Nov. 30 and runs through Dec. 6.

Recent findings suggest that with the day upon us, in-store Black Friday prices will be live at most retailers on Nov. 27. Opening are as follows:.

Best Buy: 6 a.m. local time, close at 10 p.m. local time.

In a recent development, home Depot: 6 a.m. local time, closing varies by location.

Bethany Allard is a Los Angeles-based shopping reporter at Mashable covering beauty tech, dating, sex and relationships, and headphones. That basically means she puts her hair through a lot, scrolls through a lot of dating apps, and rotates through a lot of different headphones. In addition to testing out and rounding up the best products, she also covers deals for Mashable, paying an especially obsessive amount of attention to Apple deals and prices. That knowledge comes in handy when she's covering shopping holidays like Prime Day and Black Friday, which she's now done for five years at Mashable.

Timothy Beck Werth is the Tech Editor at Mashable, where he leads coverage and assignments for the Tech and Shopping verticals. Tim has over 15 years of experience as a journalist and editor, and he has particular experience covering and testing consumer technology, smart home gadgets, and men’s grooming and style products. Previously, he was the Managing Editor and then Site Director of SPY.com, a men's product review and lifestyle website. As a writer for GQ, he covered everything from bull-riding competitions to the best Legos for adults, and he’s also contributed to publications such as The Daily Beast, Gear Patrol, and The Awl.

Tim studied print journalism at the University of Southern California. He presently splits his time between Brooklyn, NY and Charleston, SC. He's currently working on his second novel, a science-fiction book.

Industry observers note that lauren Allain is a freelance journalist covering deals at Mashable. She graduated from Western Washington University with a B.A. in journalism and holds an M.B.A from Webster Leiden. You can find more of her work online from publications including Reader’s Digest, U.S. News & World Report, Seattle Refined, and more. When she’s not writing, Lauren prefers to be outside hiking, bouldering, swimming, or searching for the perfect location for all three.

Samantha Mangino, is an e-reader expert. She's tested all the Kindle and Kobo e-readers, diving into the buzziest models. Her love of reading extends beyond the e-reader beat, covering books and authors, too. In the tech space, she covers tablets, smart rings, and headphones.

Industry News: Etsy clarifies AI terms after seller backlash
